newsitem.title: USA: Miami hires Peat Marwick to audit city finances.
newsitem.headline: Miami hires Peat Marwick to audit city finances.

text.p: Miami has hired KPMG-Peat Marwick LLP to conduct a complete audit of city finances, Acting City Manager Merrett Stierheim said Monday.
He said the finished audit is expected "shortly after the turn of the year."
The city fired its previous outside auditor, Deloitte & Touche LLP on Oct 7, alleging that the firm had failed to raise adequate warnings about the city's $68 million budget defict.
Stierheim said he and his team of 40 corporate and public finance volunteers expected to have a blueprint bail-out plan to take to the city commission around Nov 10.

We're making progress," Stierheim said. "I feel very positive that this can be managed. Obviously it's not going to be easy and it involves some sacrifices and tough political decisions. But I think it can be managed. There was a time I didn't know that and I wasn't sure."
The plan calls for fee increases, service cutbacks and concessions from city workers to close the gap in the $275 million budget for the year that began Oct 1.
Stierheim said the city had narrowed down its search for a new city manager to four candidates. He declined to identify them but described them as "a good field to select from."

Stierheim, a former Dade County manager, was appointed after city manger Cesar Odio and fianance director Manohar Surana stepped down to face federal charges that they allegedly solicited kickbacks for city contracts.
Steirheim also said he was questioned last week by investigators with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Mayor Joe Carollo previously disclosed the SEC is examining city bond issues.
"They were just asking general questions on everything I had observed in my review, how I got to where I did (on the deficit numbers)," Stierheim said.
SEC was already investigating Miami's use of bond proceeds from a December 1995 sale of $72 million of special obligation pension bonds when the budget deficit was discovered.
The city's worsening financial situation was not disclosed in bond documents for the pension bonds nor for three other bond and note issues the city sold in 1995, those involved in the sales said.

Although city commissioners said they did not know of the budget deficit until Steirheim was brought in, he said the pension bond sale should have raised red flags because proceeds were used to meet recurring annual operating costs.

"That is just not good fiscal management to issue bonds to meet yearly fiscal requirements," he said. "That's sort of a hand-to-mouth existance. That's what gave me an early indication that the city budget was not as presented, that it was in trouble."

SEC would not comment on its Miami investigation, but Stierheim said there were similarlities to the Maricopa County, Ariz., case, in which the SEC accused the county of violating securities law by failing to disclose its worsening budget deficit when it issued municipal bonds.
Maricopa County settled the charges earlier this month by agreeing to a cease and desist order.
